parole.significato: a delicate, unpleasant, or embarrassing affair
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affaire (“matter, affair; deal”) (compare English affair, Russian афе́ра (aféra)), probably also via German Affäre (“delicate or problematic affair”). First attested in 1835.
Borrowed from French assaut (possibly also via German Assaut), from Old French assaut, asalt, from Vulgar Latin *assaltus, modification of Latin assultus. First attested in 1876.

parole.significato: a loose-fitting blouse, especially for women or girls
parole.testo: Borrowed from French blouse (“uniform or coat with buttons down the front”), probably also via German Bluse (“blouse”). First attested in 1847.
Borrowed from French diseuse (“female speaker”) (could be via German Diseuse), from dire, from Latin dīcere (“to say”).

parole.significato: phenomenon (wonderful or very remarkable person or thing)
parole.testo: Internationalism, chiefly via French phénomène (“phenomenon”) and German Phänomen (“phenomenon”), ultimately from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon).
From French canapé via German Kanapee.

parole.significato: cream (a jelly-like confection made from whipped cream or milk with egg yolks and various flavourings)
parole.testo: Internationalism via French crème and German Creme.

parole.significato: synonym of kölnivíz (“cologne”, a type of perfume)
parole.testo: Ellipsis of kölni víz (“water of Cologne”) (today spelled as solid). Calque of French eau de Cologne or German Kölnisches Wasser or Kölnischwasser.

parole.significato: papier-mâché (a composite material created by pulping paper or layering paper strips with an adhesive such as glue, sta…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French papier mâché, also via German Papiermaché.

parole.significato: pardon!, pardon me!, excuse me!, I beg your pardon!, sorry!
parole.testo: From French pardon, primarily via German Pardon.
Borrowed from French roman (“novel”), also via German Roman (“novel”). Compare Serbo-Croatian ròmān /ро̀ма̄н, Czech román. First attested in 1753.

parole.significato: chic (good form, style, ease, grace and tasteful elegance, especially in women's clothing)
parole.testo: First attested in 1871. From French chic, from German Schick (“elegant appearance; tasteful presentation”).
First attested in 1837. Internationalism via French gelée (“jelly”) and German Gelee.
